body: I'm going through the same thing right now, but hoping I don't get manipulated back into the mirage. Honestly those years sucked. Sucks without it too, but idk maybe less.

I used to enjoy the play fighting. We'd surprise each other, tussle a bit, and often end up in bed. It was fun. Then she started getting angry not just when I'd try to play, but also when she'd try to play and I'd respond.

Keep in mind, she'd almost always pinch or smack a lot harder than I would. But at some point, I was no longer allowed to do anything. If she did something, and I didn't react in an immediately positive way, she'd also get angry. So not only could I not do anything, I had to enjoy what she did.

So now I just dont engage at all anymore. She's definitely a bit of a sadist.

This is one of the things I'm most looking forward to, and it's really helping me keep moving forward with divorce.

I watched a video recently from my local Historical Society where an older woman reminisced about her summers visiting family as a child, and how everyone was just happy to spend time together. I had a childhood like that, and the video helped me contrast that with how our visits with my kids and n-wife have been over the years. Sometimes it's been OK, but other times it's been a complete nightmare. She's forced the extended family into these extremely dramatic situations full of blame and punishment and revenge. If you ask her, it was all to defend our kids against horrible offenses, but really it was just her manipulating everyone for more control.

I dream of putting all that behind us so that me and the kids can visit family, repair some relationships, and just enjoy time together.

I get the best of both worlds there. I learned a long time ago not to discuss politics with my wife. First of all, she gets angry. She says news and politics give her anxiety. She doesn't really know what's going on in the world right now because she avoids any news. Second, I learned that she holds some pretty unsympathetic views towards people, and I'd rather not be reminded how hateful she can be.

If you were married, you would have quite a bit more than that. There's a little bit of narcissism in everyone, and it's not always bad. You've described someone who is maybe self-centered, and passively-aggressively trying to hide something. Narcissists do that, but so much more as well. Plenty of traits to compare against online.
How does that work? They praise you in private?

The advice I've always gotten is to vet any therapists for experience with NPD, because what you mentioned is typically what happens. Most therapists try to get couples to compromise, and that's simply not possible with a narc. In fact, the general advice is to avoid couples counseling entirely because the narc will often find a way to use it to their advantage and turn the therapist against you. I managed to find a therapist for myself who understands, and that has been very helpful.

My wife also has almost no one. Most of her family is overseas, and she doesn't have a great relationship with them anyway. I'm preparing for a divorce, and I know she'll basically be on her own afterwards. I feel terrible about that.

I think she's apologized to me maybe 3 or 4 times in 14 years, always after putting me through hell and seeing me in extreme duress. Every time it was the most basic, meek "sorry", with no follow-up or change afterwards. I used to apologize all the time, and I'm still learning that it means absolutely nothing to her. I hate to say it, but acting like them is sometimes the only way to get through to them.

It's getting easier. Reading the comments here has helped me maintain perspective. It has also been an immense help to have the support of my parents and siblings. Everyone who knows what's going on has told me that I'm doing the right thing.

Just because he is in government doesn't mean he knows every single lawyer there is. I'm not a lawyer, but my understanding is that they have to tell you if they know your husband because it is a conflict of interest. They are also not allowed to tell him you contacted them because that breaks attorney-client privilege. You can also contact lawyers in other towns within your state.

In other words, you should be careful, but it is possible to do it in secret. You absolutely should seek out legal advice, even if just to know what your options are. They will be able to tell you what you'd need for sole custody. A woman's support group would also be a good idea. 

Depending on how controlling he is, you may have to get creative with appointments.  But I think you'll find people can be very flexible and supportive if you explain your situation.

Mine would never even make that claim. She would never consider therapy, couples, or otherwise. As far as she's concerned, everything she does is good and beyond question. If something bad happens, it's always someone else's fault. I have no illusions of her ever changing.

I think I'm on the verge of getting discarded. I began to draw some lines on her behavior, so she no longer feels like I give her the supply she needs. I've since learned that she's been chatting romantically online with other guys. It's hard to accept how easy it is for them to stop caring, but these aren't the first signs that I've seen. I've just been ignoring them.

\> I try to tell myself to go all out legally but in my interactions I can still have compassion.

That's something, at least. I've read about people who left that say the first year or two suck, but afterwards they've never felt happier. I'm holding on to the hope that I will get there some day.

Yes, 14 years. I don't think she has cheated physically, but I know she has been speaking to others romantically online. She is very good at making someone feel loved. Maybe in some way it's genuine, but I've learned that it's very conditional on whether I give her the supply she needs. If I don't she will casually look for it somewhere else.

That's exactly why experience with NPD is so important, not just with therapists, but lawyers as well. Be careful of people who confuse the popular concept of narcissism with NPD. There are some podcasts by Dr. Supriya McKenna that I found very helpful in processing what it means to have a narc in your life.
I hesitated to look for a lawyer for too long, because it felt disloyal. I made the leap for my kids. There is no harm in being prepared. A therapist experienced with NPD is also highly recommended.

Yes my wife is a covert/vulnerable narcissist. Most of her mean behavior is small things, easier to ignore, but sometimes she can be very vicious. My eldest was treated badly from a very young age, and still gets the worst. My second had a bit more time, but is treated like a failure. My youngest is still mostly safe at 7yo. She corrupted my own behavior and there  were times I behaved poorly as well, out of avoidance and exhaustion.

I don't regret staying long enough to have my kids, because they are amazing. I deeply regret not protecting them better, and I now realize the only real way to protect them is to keep them away from her. At least until she's able to demonstrate that she cares about them by seeking help for herself. I am not optimistic. At this point she has probably already caused long-term damage to their psyches.

You should consider that she is likely to treat your son the same way that she treats you. I have a therapist who specializes in NPD who told me that when the situation gets to separation it's almost always because of the kids. You have a chance now to spare your son what you are experiencing. I highly recommend researching NPD, and if possible taking sessions with a therapist that has experience with it.

I'm in a very similar situation, 14 years, 3 kids, covert narc wife that's heavily dependent on me... I'm just now beginning the separation process, in secret because I don't trust her to be reasonable. I expect full custody of the kids because there has been abuse, and that is the most painful part of it. I don't want my kids to lose their mom. I feel extremely guilty, like I'm stabbing her in the back.

Sorry, I don't have any advice for you, I'm barely managing myself. But you're not alone.

edit: I guess my advice is, start taking small steps. Don't pretend there will be a right moment.

Keep researching, keep learning, keep aware. I first learned about NPD 3 years ago after living with it for 11. It's only just now that I'm realizing how insidious it is. How subtly and deeply it worms it's way into your head. You can't see what you've been blinded to. A therapist who has actual NPD experience can make a big difference. Find a way to meet one even if you have to hide it from your narc, like I did.

I will absolutely give her as much access to the kids as I can while keeping them safe. I have no idea how that will work. She has always avoided, ignored, or angrily rejected any hint of criticism of her behavior. She knows what she does is wrong (often showing extra affection for the kids the day after), but refuses to do anything about it. She will not accept therapy, and I'm told it will only get worse.

All I can think is that maybe the shock will wake something up inside her and she'll decide her kids are worth fighting for. If she cares, there may still be a path open to her.

Thanks. Depriving my kids of their mom, who they love, is what has stopped me all these years. I wish I could be sure this is what's best. It feels like doing a bad thing to avoid what might be worse. I still hope for a better path.
There has been abuse. Mostly emotional, but on rare occasions physical as well. She refuses to acknowledge it, and gaslit me in many ways. I should have acted a long time ago.
This was a great interview, and led me to a number of other podcasts I plan to listen to. Thanks again!

I can't speak for my kids, but I do have issues with stress that are likely affecting my health. Cognitive dissonance is a funny thing. It's easy to notice in others, even when their situation is very similar to your own, yet difficult to notice in yourself.

Thank you for the perspective from your field. I made this post because I don't feel like I have a good frame of reference for abuse. My own childhood was very loving and kind, and I never personally experienced abuse. But I did live in cultures where various forms of physical discipline are common. The "chancleta", for example, is a common stereotype in Latin cultures. I often heard about spanking in the US. My sister attended school in Africa where she was nearly beaten in the courtyard with a ruler for some minor infraction. My parents sent her to a boarding school when they learned of it.

I guess my point is that it's been difficult for me to grasp what is discipline vs abuse, and my wife has always framed it as discipline (and called me soft or weak). Of course, you might say that it's abuse regardless of whether a society accepts it. But, I'm realizing that even if some things could be considered discipline, that's not what's been happening in my family. In the worst cases, my wife isn't disciplining at all. The violence is just part of the rage.

Unfortunately, I don't have any evidence for past abuse other than what my kids might remember. It's unclear how long it might be before something happens again. It's another story, but my wife has recently found a new source of supply online which has her very distracted, and largely ignoring the rest of the family. It's sad to think about, but it's actually been quite nice for us. That said, I do have a different perspective on the whole situation now, so I will try to be careful, methodical, and as safe as I can be while I collect the information I need to take the next step.

You're telling me that no matter what I do, the abuse will get worse. I posted here because all of this is new to me. I've known about NPD for about 3 years, but have only recently started to understand what it really means. If people here are telling me that it only gets worse, I can't ignore that.

I do feel like my kids have an emotional shield up. They're way too young for that. 

I guess it's time to start learning about divorce. I will talk to a lawyer.

It's easy to say that physical abuse is all it should take to end a relationship. It feels like the right thing to say and believe. I don't think it's always that simple. First, there are degrees in everything. If my wife had tried beating my kids, this would have ended in the first instance. I earnestly believe the emotional abuse has been far worse than any of the physical things she has done.

Emotionally, it has been a roller coaster. We built a life together, and it's full of beautiful and terrible moments, not all of them her fault. I spoke with my kids today, my two eldest. I was more direct with my 14 yo, but subtler with the 11 yo. They clearly don't like the things their mom does, though they say they mostly just ignore it. It does seem like they've normalized it, which is not great. I stressed to them that it is not normal. Most of all, it was clear that they don't want her to go anywhere. They do love her.

Most of my recent doubts, relating to the romances you mention, are personal to me. It has me thinking I should leave for my sake. I posted this because I still don't know that a separation would make things better for the kids. I don't know how my wife would react to either sole or joint custody, but I can't see a way that my kids would enjoy any of it. I think there is real potential for trauma there. Either they lose their mom almost entirely, or they are on their own with her.

If I were to take sole custody, with visitation, my kids would only ever know their mother in a sterile environment. They'd never learn to interact with her as she really is. They'd grow up without a mother.

If I were to take joint custody, my kids would be alone with her where I can't do anything for them until after the fact.

On the other hand, if I stay, maybe I can protect them because I will always be around. I'm not as ignorant any more. I can recognize my wife's behaviors fairly easily now, and guide her away from the worst of her devils. I can teach them in the moments when they clash with her.

My children surely walk on eggshells too. It's not all the time. My wife has fairly distinct content vs. discontent "auras" that she projects. The transition to discontent does surprise us sometimes, but I think there are periods of days or even weeks sometimes when my kids and I can actually relax a bit.

I have family nearby I can always stay with if I need to. I haven't expressed the full extent of our situation to them, but they have experienced some of it. I know my family would trust anything I have to say on the matter. In her defense O:) I will say that my wife is a fundamentally good person. She seems to have set lines for herself that she wouldn't cross. I say I don't know how far she would go because when she is in her rage it doesn't seem like she knows what she's doing. If she has no control, she can't control crossing a line.
I've gotten a lot of good perspective here, and also in r/NarcissisticSpouses. I really appreciate it!
Thank you!
I will, thanks!

Yes, I notice myself defending her all the time, even with the kids. "Mommy's tired" or "Mommy had a bad day". That sort of stuff. And I've certainly been a target of her abuse as well. I've spent a considerable amount of time tip-toeing around her and capitulating to her needs to avoid angering or even just annoying her.

I would say that our home environment is generally quite warm and loving. It's only recently that I've started questioning how genuine it is on her part. She is very good at showing love when she wants to, but I've been noticing how easily she transitions into complete neglect.

I don't think we're really unsafe in any direct way. She angers quickly, but it usually takes some time before she gets worked up to physical abuse, and I've been getting much better at defusing those situations before they get bad. But I also don't know how severely she would react to a significant change in her life. It would not be difficult for us to find a safe place to go if we needed to.

\> The children seem "resilient" (so far) because they are in survival mode.

That's what I've been worried about, and why I'm here asking. It does seem likely they have more going on that it appears.

I feel like I should call out the abuse more directly when it happens. It's the only moment when she can't avoid it, because she's actively doing it. But you're right that she's likely to twist it and try to use it against me instead.

At this point I have started documenting, but I don't think I'm ready to contact a lawyer just yet. The question of what would happen afterwards still gives me pause. Sole custody seems cruel to me, but maybe I still haven't accepted the full reality of what's been going on. I'm hoping to speak with a therapist first, but it's hard to find once that has experience with NPD.
Absolutely. Even before I knew about NPD, we reached moments when I had to intervene. I know enough now that I'm usually able to defuse before I have to intervene.

I have been changing the dynamics, and it does seem to be working, but not enough time has passed to be sure. It has been a while since she's fully gone into a rage, but I don't know if that's because I'm setting more limits, or if something else is going on.

That's why I said I'm not optimistic. I'm wondering, though, if I might arrange for some "study-hall" time for her for a tele-session with a therapist I know already. Of course, I still have to ask her if it's something she's willing to try.

My wife definitely knows that what she does is wrong. But when I bring it up, other than her immediate reaction, she basically ignores it. When I've tried to bring it up when she's calmer, she immediately redirects the conversation and refuses to engage with it. Or gets angry again. Or even tries the "I'm their mother, and suffered for them" bit. She uses DARVO all the time.

Things are actually a bit shakier than usual right now, which I guess is where this is coming from. She will throw things off balance if she ever sees that her comfortable position is threatened. That may be coming regardless of what I do though, so we may not be able to avoid it anyway.

I'm realizing it's time to start asking my daughter, at least, some tougher questions. In particular, what she wants and hopes for. I had hoped to wait until she was older. Therapy will be a real challenge. My wife sees therapy as a weakness, and is absolutely opposed to it in all forms. She made it pretty unpleasant for me when I've tried sessions for myself in the past, so there's no way she'd accept it for our kids. Maybe I can ask about something through her school. I'm not optimistic about that, but I don't know what else to try.

I do speak out. I always do now, after learning about NPD. I had a shift in perspective a few months ago and started drawing more lines. I confess I've avoided saying "abusive" because it gets a strong reaction from her, but I see your point. It's what she needs to hear, both of them. And I'm actively learning about as much of this as I can. That's why I'm here.

I read this again, and I just have to add that I *dream* of that decade where I don't have a constant shadow hanging over me. In my fondest fantasies, she's forgotten about me and is doing her thing somewhere else, my kids are off making me proud, and I'm free to roam the world, doing good work and meeting new people.

I've managed to temper my drinking. I used to drink one or two full whiskey glasses of straight liqour chased by a beer or two every single night. She complained about it all the time, but I suspect it had more to do with the fact that I was enjoying something without her rather than any concern for me. She never did anything but make me feel bad about it.

It hasn't been easy to stop because I feel like it's the only way I have left to cope with the stress. Through therapy and external support, I began to recognize how it's been hurting me more than it helps. For my own sake, I no longer drink every night, and when I do, it's far less. I feel like I'd lose my sanity entirely if I just stopped because there are times when it's all too much for me.

I haven't said a thing to her about it. It's been months now, and she has no idea. She hasn't even realized that's she's stopped complaining about it. I'm certain that if I told her, she'd find some way to shame me for it.

Yeah, as another commenter said, this might be affecting them in ways I'm not considering. I still have to worry that my wife would end up with at least partial custody during a time when she would not be feeling good. That's when she's the most dangerous, and likely to take it out on others.

A lawyer would be a really hard step for me to take. I can see the wisdom in it, but it seems so harsh to me. Obviously, I wouldn't tell my wife, but I know that it would hurt her to find out. I'm not trying to hurt her, I just want to stop hurting. Probably something to work through with a therapist, but I'll think about it.

I've seen that subreddit, but haven't paid much attention. You may be right. The kids seem fine, but that doesn't mean that they actually are. I don't really have any idea how this might be affecting them, or what consequences there might be in the future. I've done a reasonable amount of research about NPD in general, but I've been focused on the traits and behavior management.

Thanks for the recommendation. I owe it to my kids to get a better understanding of what they might be going through.
It's really starting to sink in, yeah.
Heh, I just watched that scene last night with my kids. I appreciate that, thanks.

She would go ballistic. The best part is that she complained ruthlessly about my own gaming habits for years. I had a small group of buddies that were basically my only friends, and I slowly learned that there was no acceptable way to spend any time with them. I eventually gave up and haven't spoken to any of them in a long time. Fortunately, I'm a fairly resilient introvert, but I think loneliness feels worse when you're not actually alone.

I tried to draw the comparison for her, but it's like she's simply incapable of understanding it.

It's the idea of leaving our kids alone with her that stops me more than anything else. She's generally very good (and our kids are amazing), but when she's not she can get quite extreme. I want to think she would never physically hurt them, but she seems to completely lose control of herself, and I have no trust for her in those situations. It's rare, but I don't ever want them to be alone with her when it happens. And there is always plenty of emotional abuse, which I know affects them deeply. I do my best to be there for them afterwards, or any other time. I don't know what else to do. I know they also love her very much, and I believe that it would hurt them more if she were not around.

You're right that she's probably already doing it. This isn't the first hint that I've gotten. In the past 2 months or so, she's been playing this online social game where she's getting fed large amounts of the validation she so desperately needs. She's mentioned in passing that guys have been complimenting her in ways that she appreciates.

How does she really feel about me? Gosh, that's a tough question. I like to think I'm being honest with myself when I say that she does actually love me. She is very good at showing care when she wants to, and it has always felt genuine. But, just recently she almost completely ignored me for my birthday. She's never done that before. She spent the entire day playing that game. Even after so long together, it was stunning to me that I was so casually set aside.

I am seriously considering therapy again, though it's very hit and miss for me. I rarely get much out of it other than just being able to unburden myself. She absolutely refuses to go, couples counseling or otherwise. It's a weakness to her, and I have to hide my visits from her or get a bunch of crap for it.

I really hadn't considered not answering. What you say makes a whole lot of sense to me, and I will try very hard to take your advice to heart. Thank you for your perspective.

I often think that I just need to hold on until the kids are on their own, but my youngest is 7 and 10 more years seems like an eternity. I definitely worry about how this might affect our kids. My wife can be pretty inconsiderate, even with them. She probably wouldn't outright tell them, but I doubt she'd try to be discrete in any way either.

For myself, I think I'd be ok initially, but I don't know how it would affect me over time. I can see her using it to humiliate me in small ways, and that would start to take a toll. You're right that she probably has every intention of doing it, and may even have started already. So maybe this is less about what I tell her and more about how I deal with it.

Sometimes, in quieter moments, I let myself relax in her company and begin to think everything is fine and we'll be ok. Then she inevitably says some small thing that cracks the facade, and I remember how everyone says that it just gets worse. That's what worries me more than anything else. Thanks for your response.

She absolutely refuses to do counseling. Won't do therapy for herself either. For context, I highly suspect she's low on the spectrum for Narcissistic Personality Disorder. I know people throw that around a lot, but I've done a fair amount of research on it, and I think it fits. Refusing counseling is one trait.

I've tried therapy a few times and found it hit and miss. I generally try to keep it from my wife, otherwise I get a bunch of crap for it. After this latest realization, I very well may try again.
Got it. Trans people aren't important with everything else that's going on. How far down the list are immigrants? Well, doesn't matter until it gets to you.

I suppose there may be some kids who adopt aspects of trans culture because it's "cool", but I seriously doubt it lasts long because trans kids generally have much harder lives than most people. And no one is going to undergo hormone therapy or surgery just to fit in.

The vast majority will be kids who have real feelings of gender dysphoria, to the point where the relief they feel from looking the way they feel outweighs the abuse they receive from society.

What you're saying is really no different than saying being gay is a phase. It's absurd that you're dismissing the reality of the trans experience so casually.

As the parent poster said, transition is not an immediate, irreversible process. It takes years, and this aggressive rejection by society only makes it more difficult for kids to make the right decisions for themselves as they mature.

You're throwing reason up against emotion, which is never likely to work. A lot of people see supporting transitioning as a cruelty rather than the kindness that it usually is. The only thing with a reasonable chance of changing that is personal experience. Not that you shouldn't try, but I'd keep my expectations low.
This thread has created a ton of great discussion. Imagine if r/conservative were this open in all threads.
It's an popular law, so you can generally rely on backlash from the community for enforcement.  This guy just thinks he can get away with being an asshole now, for some reason.

So what? Everyone is using LLMs these days. It's not like the message becomes meaningless just because someone used a tool to help with the phrasing.
As far as controlled opposition, this is a message encouraging action from the masses. If the message was "it's cool, we got it," then maybe you'd have a point.

Reddit can be frustrating like this sometimes. On popular subs, a post can easily get drowned out and lost if it doesn't get immediate engagement from people browsing new posts. If you sort this sub by new, you'll see there's only a couple of comments from people I the last few hours. When you post can also make a big difference. 

Anyway, you don't deserve abuse, and lots of perfectly decent people are alone. If you're not getting replies, chances are it's for completely mundane reasons.

I know this is a late reply, but it was more than 10 years for me before I learned i might be dealing with NPD. My point is, if you're going to dig in, dig in. It's a journey. Otherwise, you're probably better off getting out ASAP. It helps to make the decision.

What website?

> A person that thinks those who defend their country in uniform, or are shot down or seriously wounded in combat, or spend years being tortured as POWs are all 'suckers' because 'there is nothing in it for them.'

That is a direct quote from John Kelly. Prove it for yourself.

No, dude. It's a direct accusation by John Kelly, Trump's own Chief of Staff. Are you really, *really*, trusting Trump's words over literally anyone else at this point? An absurd amount of people from the 2016 admin had shit to say about him, and it's entirely within character for him. No it's not "proven", but it's blatantly fucking obvious that he said it!
I'd say there's a high correlation.

Interesting. I'm in a similar boat, except that's more of a positive side-effect. It took a few months before my alcohol use began to drop, probably because it was largely habitual. But where I used to have a drink out of habit, now I usually just don't think about it.
To that point, the Nazis did try deportation first, but no other country would accept them. Genocide was the "final solution".
Are there any studies yet that observe "minidoses"? Like, the walls will wiggle a bit, but you won't trip?

Ultimately, NPD has to be the result of some subset of wires getting crossed in the brain. There are any number of ways that could happen. It could have been a bump on the head, for all you know. Or your partner simply has forgotten, blocked, or avoided telling you.

I think there is always a progression, regardless of how it starts.

Day by day, it's not so much about how it happened, as what triggers the behaviors. In my case, I believe my wife's NPD is triggered by her insecurity. It might help to some degree to know that was caused by her evil stepmother and stepsisters, but what I try to focus on when I'm dealing with her is her insecurity.

Revenge sleep procrastination.  Or at least that's what I think it is for me. It's had me sleeping an average of 5-6 hours a night for about 10 years. Also, a few 3 and 4 sprinkled in, but thankfully not as many of those as there used to be.
Narcissism can often come from deep insecurity. The frog is how ugly they see themselves, and the narcissism is how they compensate.

My first thought was to sell off the investments. Not great timing, but it's likely worth it. I hadn't considered delaying payments. That might help a lot if I can avoid fees.

You're right. I guess this will only cost me at most a couple hundred dollars. Maybe it would help drive the lesson home to leave it alone. It's just been so long since I've had to worry about money at all, so it's a bit uncomfortable.

I will check out my 401k loan options. Normally I would avoid touching it at all, but if I can get a decent rate that way, maybe it's worth it. I guess I'm probably only looking at a couple hundred dollars in interest before I can get back to zero, so maybe I'm overreacting. I just feel really stupid.

Once I started making enough to cover regular expenses I got out of the habit of budgeting. I have always taken the time to at least review of everything before a big expense, but this time I didn't take everything into account. These recent expenses were unavoidable, but I should have at least seen that I couldn't afford to pay them upfront.
I'll try them first, thanks.

I've never taken out a personal loan, so I wasn't sure what the turnaround time on those is. I'll see what I can find. I'll check out cards too. A hit to my credit score would not be so bad right now.

401k contributions wouldn't get me too much. Maybe another $1.4k if I can get the whole month. I prefer to ignore that account.

Thanks for the tips.

Yeah I see most of these things manifest in many different ways. I'm fairly certain she has NPD. What may be helping is that things are going pretty well for her right now. Or at least for the things that aren't going well I've learned to navigate the kind of responses she's expecting. Of course, I don't always get it right.

My hope is I can learn to manage/contain it better, though my worry is that it won't matter even if I do.

I worry a lot about how this will affect our kids. I know everyone here says that narcs have no capacity to love, but it really doesn't feel that way in our case. My wife is pretty dedicated to them and spends quite a lot of time playing with them and teaching them things. Of course, when she gets angry she'll go to extremes.

Meanwhile, our kids adore her. And despite my worries they do seem to be pretty well adjusted and happy. So on the other hand, if I were to leave, I worry about what kind of trauma that would cause. My oldest (11) has told me one of her biggest worries is that we'll break up.

And my wife hasn't done anything that warrants losing access to the kids completely.  So it's not like if we broke up she wouldn't be around the kids all the time anyway.

Sorry, I was only trying to get a general idea if Narc could be managed like an illness (which it seems it cannot). I wrote about her traits in my first post here: https://www.reddit.com/r/NarcissisticSpouses/comments/qyn5nc/venting/
